KEY MESSAGE 1...Diminishing winds and clearing tonight with cold 
low temps in the 20s and 30s with widespread frost/freeze conditions. 
Sunshine returns on Sunday with highs in the 50s with light winds.

Model cross sections indicate that lingering mid level cloudiness 
pushes south of the region tonight. This combined with high pressure 
building in from the west coupled with diminishing winds and a dry 
airmass in place will set the stage for a cold night. Low temps 
should bottom out in the middle to upper 20s in many locations with 
lower to middle 30s common in the urban heat islands as well as the 
Cape/Nantucket where winds will not decouple. Widespread 
frost/freeze conditions expected...But our Frost/Freeze program has 
ended already so no headlines needed.

High pressure will result in sunny skies for Sunday. High temps will 
be in the 50s...which is a bit below normal for this time of year. 
However...with very little wind outside the Cape/Islands it will 
feel significantly milder by afternoon than today. 

High pressure remains in control of our weather Sunday night with 
mainly clear skies. This will result in another good night of 
radiational cooling with lows in the 20s and 30s.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Mainly dry for the upcoming workweek except near 
coastal areas. Otherwise, the other big story is a modest warming 
trend with high pressure building in across the Northeastern United 
States. 

General theme for the long term forecast is the return of drier and 
somewhat warmer conditions going into the workweek as a broad ridge 
of high pressure develops over the CONUS. Outside of this, guidance 
continues to indicate the development of low pressure towards the 
mid-Atlantic/Carolina coastal waters later Sunday into the day on 
Monday. Ironically, this feature stems from last night's cold front 
as it continues to move offshore and stall into a stationary 
boundary. At the same time, lingering upper level energy cuts off 
and induces the development of a frontal wave off the coast of the 
Carolinas later Saturday night into Sunday morning. Still see a 
signal for enough of a weakness in the ridge for low pressure to 
move N and affect coastal areas Monday and Tuesday. Have continued 
to see drier solutions with this storm as a dry airmass precedes the 
northward precip shield. 12z global guidance QPF looks quite 
limited, with ensemble probabilities for any measurable rainfall 
mostly between 10-50%, with the GEFS and Canadian ENS skewing 
slightly higher over the Cape and Islands at 50-60%. The ECMWF 
ensemble is the lowest of the three, with the highest probabilities 
over land being 10-30%. However, marine impacts with this 
disturbance are looking a bit more impactful as it stays relatively 
stationary and churns over the same waters for an extended period of 
time, which will help build seas up to 15 ft offshore of Nantucket.
 
The gradient between this area of low pressure and the preexisting 
high pressure over southern New England will tighten greatly, 
increasing ENE winds over the waters and towards the Cape and 
Islands, RI, and the coastal plain in SE MA. Ensembles have 
continued to indicate decent probabilities of sustained winds 
reaching gale-force over the southern waters, with the GEFS and 
Canadian ensemble up to 30-40% (and even up to 60% in the Canadian 
guidance) just south of the Islands. In terms of gale- force gusts, 
probabilities have increased further from the last update, reaching 
the high (80-100%) range in the ECMWF ensemble and up to 80% in the 
GEFS. Persistent easterly fetch associated with these winds, along 
with building rough seas, will need to be monitored as well, as 
beach erosion for east- and northeast- facing beaches may become an 
issue.
